item.title: Trump Outlines Rapid Plan to Close and Overhaul D.C. Golf Course
item.description:
President Trump said on Sunday that his administration had finalized plans to transform East Potomac Golf Links in Washington into a “World Class Championship Golf Course,” saying the municipal course would close within four weeks and that its replacement would be playable in about 15 months.

The announcement set up another frantic legal clash over the site. A federal judge ordered the administration in July to present her with any long-term plans for the course and not to carry out a surprise overhaul as the president had with the East Wing of the White House and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The Interior Department appeared to have done just that earlier this month, taking down hundreds of trees over a holiday weekend and giving the court and a group suing to stop any changes to the course less than a day to react.

In a post on social media on Sunday morning, Mr. Trump appeared to affirm what a historical-preservation group and two Washington residents had warned of in a federal lawsuit: that the administration might move to seize the existing course before they had a real chance to oppose the plan.

Mr. Trump wrote that he had already notified professional golf organizations that “they will soon have one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World to put on their list of great places to play, and hold Major Events.” He added that he had secured a design by Tom Fazio, a well-known designer who has planned other courses owned by the Trump Organization.

The president shared a rendering of the planned course that resembled a blurred-out image sitting on his desk in a photo shared on Friday by Katie Zacharia, his press secretary who was ousted from the role after less than a week.

In response to the post, Judge Ana C. Reyes, who has presided over the case, ordered the Justice Department to reconcile the announcement with what had been said in court by Sunday at 8 p.m.

She noted that the government had consistently denied that any decisions on the future of the course had been made along the lines of the vision Mr. Trump has shared publicly. She quoted a Justice Department lawyer who, as recently as Friday, said that Mr. Trump “at most” had given only “preliminary thought to” the future of the course.

The group opposing the plan has argued that the existing course provided an affordable and accessible option to players in the Washington area who would be harmed by its conversion into a more exclusive, professional-level destination. Critics and local golfers have also expressed doubt that the isolated Hains Point peninsula, where the course is situated, could handle the traffic that professional tournaments would demand.

The map Mr. Trump shared on Sunday showed the new course covering the bulk of East Potomac Park, with the proposed 12th hole situated over what is now a public picnic area and playground at Hains Point. In addition to the current municipal course, the perimeter of the island is also a popular cycling circuit.

“East Potomac Park is a national park, golf course and recreational facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy,” said Skye Perryman, the president of Democracy Forward, which is representing the group challenging the plan. “Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves.”

Mr. Trump has signaled for months that he intended to realize the plan, and he was photographed touring the site and studying blueprints with Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Mr. Fazio in June.

But because there had not previously been imminent plans to move forward with the redevelopment, Judge Reyes was hesitant for months to preemptively block the Trump administration from making any changes to the existing course. Instead, she had prevailed upon the Justice Department to notify her before making any major changes.

During a hearing in July, a Justice Department lawyer said that no decision had been reached on the fate of the course.

After it was revealed that the Interior Department cleared hundreds of trees last weekend, Judge Reyes excoriated the Justice Department for failing to keep her apprised during a fiery hearing on Monday. She accused the government of “double speak” for representing in court that the work was planned maintenance, despite Mr. Trump’s public vision to transform the course.

Seething at a government lawyer, Judge Reyes turned an extended portion of the four-hour hearing into an effort to identify who had given the go-ahead to begin the work. She ordered the government to track down several senior officials in the Interior Department to testify on the spot but was able to reach only one.

Judge Reyes lamented that she had tried to avoid “playing parks and rec” or policing landscaping decisions at the course. But confronted with signs that the administration was rushing forward, she ordered the government not to remove any more trees until Oct. 26 to give the group opposing the plan time to respond.

The question of who authorized the work is expected to be the focus of a hearing on Monday, at which Judge Reyes had ordered Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee at the Interior Department, and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify.

But the Justice Department escalated the standoff on Friday and filed a motion to disqualify Judge Reyes, citing her frustration at the hearing in order to question her impartiality and ask that she recuse herself from the case. She ordered both sides to file a response to the request by Sunday afternoon.

On Sunday, Judge Reyes also ordered Stanley Woodward Jr., the associate attorney general who filed the motion to disqualify her, to attend the hearing on Monday in which more senior Interior Department officials are scheduled to testify.

In the post on Sunday, Mr. Trump repeated an argument the government had made in court that clearing trees from the course was meant to return it to its original 1920s design, which featured open sight lines. But while the government indicated last week that the tree removal was proposed in a seven-year-old historic-restoration concept, Mr. Trump appeared to suggest that it was linked to the “Fazio Design” that he said would be built starting on Nov. 15.

item.title: The 2028 Presidential ‘Shadow Primary’ Descends on the Midterms
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom of California spent his Saturday weaving through New Hampshire, campaigning with midterm candidates as he faced questions about his presidential ambitions. Next weekend, former Vice President Kamala Harris, who is weighing another White House bid, plans to be in the state with the Democratic Senate nominee. And days after that, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, who is also considering a run, will appear there, too.

In the final stage of this year’s midterms, prospective presidential candidates are parachuting into battleground states to rally support for candidates on the ballot this fall, road-test their stump speeches, and introduce themselves to voters and activists. The Democratic schedule is especially packed in New Hampshire, an early presidential nominating state where there is a competitive Senate race. While New Hampshire has lost its long vaunted first-in-the-nation Democratic primary status to South Carolina, it will go third in 2028.

“Got here last night from the most un-Trump state in the United States of America, California,” Mr. Newsom told the crowd in Exeter, N.H., at a rally on Saturday with Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate nominee, as well as other Democratic candidates. His 10-minute speech focused primarily on Mr. Trump.

Ambitious Republicans, too, are trying to leave lasting marks across the country in this year’s high-stakes elections. Vice President JD Vance and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas are hitting the road for midterm candidates, including in states expected to figure prominently in the next G.O.P. presidential race.

In both parties, the possible presidential candidates’ itineraries reflect their standings, showing where they are in demand and where they are not. At times, midterm candidates have subtly or loudly distanced themselves from some of them.

In other cases, midterm contenders have welcomed the extra attention and support. Mr. Newsom’s trip to New Hampshire follows recent visits by Senator Raphael Warnock, Democrat of Georgia, and Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, among others. Mr. Pappas, whose roster of surrogates from outside New Hampshire has grown, is facing former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican.

“I think of political campaigns like building a house. You have to build the foundation first before building the walls. That’s what these visits are,” said Jim Demers, a veteran New Hampshire Democratic strategist, who like other operatives refers to the current phase as the “shadow primary.”

At the town hall event in Exeter, Mr. Newsom popped out from behind a curtain, beaming as Macklemore and Ryan Lewis’s “Can’t Hold Us” played in the background. Asked about his political future, he waved his hand and said, “It’s all about 2026.”

While others similarly say they are solely focused on this year’s elections, Democratic and Republican strategists see multiple purposes in these visits.

“A campaign for president is like having an endoscopy and a colonoscopy at the same time,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist. “A lot of candidates are truly deciding whether they want to do this.”

Midterm travel may be especially attractive to lesser-known politicians looking to raise their national profiles, and to those who don’t hold public office.

Mr. Buttigieg, who left his post in the Biden administration in early 2025, has endorsed more than 100 candidates this cycle and campaigned for them in more than 30 states. Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky has headlined Democratic Party dinners or conventions in nine states, including several that will hold early presidential primaries. Representative Ro Khanna of California has campaigned for more than 70 candidates.

Others have been more selective with their travels. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, recently campaigned in Michigan, another early-nominating state, with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate. She plans to appear in Maine this week with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee there.

The country faces a “pivotal and consequential moment,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said in Michigan on Friday. She brushed aside speculation about her 2028 plans, saying, “What matters right now is the next 19 days.”

Ms. Harris also recently appeared with Dr. El-Sayed. She plans to visit Nevada, an early-nominating state, as well as Mississippi, Georgia and Wisconsin.

But Senate candidates in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas have publicly and pre-emptively uninvited Ms. Harris, whose ties to the Biden administration have made her unwelcome in some conservative-leaning states.

Tensions have flared in other ways. In recent weeks, Latino leaders became angry that the Democratic Governors Association, chaired by Mr. Beshear, was not investing more money into Gina Hinojosa’s race for Texas governor against Greg Abbott, the Republican incumbent. They made veiled threats to withhold their support from Mr. Beshear should he run for president in 2028.

Within a week, the D.G.A. made a seven-figure donation to help elect Ms. Hinojosa.

Some potential presidential candidates have sought to balance their own re-elections: Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania are on the ballot in November. Mr. Shapiro recently started a federal political-action committee that enables him to give money to congressional candidates.

On the Republican side, Mr. Vance has campaigned in Kansas, Michigan and other battlegrounds. In Michigan on Thursday, he called the Senate contest “the most important race in the United States of America,” as he stumped for Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee.

Mr. Trump’s sinking approval ratings have made the president and, by extension, Mr. Vance a liability for some battleground candidates, as they seek to energize the party’s base voters. When Mr. Vance held a rally in Iowa last month, Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate, didn’t attend, citing scheduling conflicts.

Republican “candidates in swing seats want his voters, not necessarily his baggage,” said Matt Klink, a Republican strategist in California, speaking of Mr. Trump.

Mr. Cruz, who has clashed publicly with Mr. Vance, has raised money and campaigned in his home state of Texas for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in a tight contest, and visited Iowa, which has been an early Republican nominating state, among other places.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a frequent target in Democrats’ campaign attacks, has also campaigned for Republicans this cycle in Iowa and Kentucky, a departure from past Pentagon officials who have stayed out of politics.

In New Hampshire, Derek Thibeault, 55, the chair of the Nashua Democratic City Committee, said he approached Mr. Newsom at an event on Saturday and asked the governor to let him know when he’d be back to campaign for the White House.

“He gave me a big laugh, but he didn’t say no,” Mr. Thibeault said.

Andrew Sylvia contributed reporting from New Hampshire.

item.title: Larry David Mocks the D.S.A. Some Are Not Amused.
item.description:
The last time Larry David waded into politics with a satirical essay, it was to take aim at a very safe target in his liberal circles — President Trump.

Mr. David, who is known for his brand of anxious, observational comedy, mocked Bill Maher for dining with Mr. Trump at the White House in a guest essay published in The New York Times Opinion section last year headlined “My Dinner With Adolf,” in which he imagined dining with Hitler in 1939.

But Mr. David’s latest satire took aim at topics that are likely to be far more controversial within the coastal enclaves where his work is popular: the ascendant Democratic Socialists of America and its hostility toward Israel.

In a new essay published by Air Mail, the 79-year old comic channels the satirist Jonathan Swift and offers a dozen “modest proposals” for the manifesto of the socialist organization, whose actual proposals and guiding principles have been widely debated this year as several candidates aligned with the organization won primaries.

Mr. David’s suggestions start with ideas rooted in core planks of the movement, as he parodies proposals to abolish prisons and restrictions on immigration.

“In our Socialist America,” Mr. David writes, “everyone will be so fulfilled spiritually and financially that the police department will be dramatically reduced to where an officer’s only job will be to adjudicate domestic disputes.”

“Toward that end, stands will be set up at local farmers markets, where they will work to resolve marital issues in a folksy, farm-to-table manner,” he writes.

He rapidly progresses to more outlandish ideas, including national paid leave for the death of pets, mandating that employers provide cots for two siestas a day, allowing humans who identify as animals to “relieve themselves” wherever they wish and reparations that would enlist white people to serve as slaves for Black families.

Mr. David then aims his pen at one of the biggest fault lines dividing the Democratic Party, wading into the fraught debate over the line between opposition to Israel and antisemitism. Jews, he writes, will no longer be allowed to call themselves “the Chosen people” — a part of Jewish identity dating back millenniums — and will be known instead as “the Bagel People.”

“We strongly believe in a two-state solution,” the proposal says. “To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful and grapefruits are aplenty. We think the Bagel People will be very happy there.”

Best known for the hit TV shows “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” Mr. David has long been a prominent Democratic donor in Hollywood with an interest in political satire.

A national spokesperson for the D.S.A. declined to comment on Mr. David’s article. But online, some took umbrage at Mr. David’s satire of the democratic socialists. Matthew Gauna, a 29-year-old student in San Antonio who agrees with D.S.A. ideas but said he is not a member of the organization, replied online to a post comparing Mr. David to Mr. Maher by calling Mr. David “my problematic king,” with a wilted flower emoji.

“I don’t know if Larry is on top of his comedic game right now,” Mr. Gauna said in a phone interview.

Another post described the essay as “Larry David has a boomer crashout over Israel.”

Zack Wall, 35, of Columbus, Ohio, replied online to that post, writing, “Someone take the phone from gramps,” along with three crying-face emojis.

Mr. Wall said in a phone interview that Mr. David’s piece was an “utter disappointment.”

“Not so much that he was ragging on D.S.A. I don’t care about that part,” said Mr. Wall, who added that he identifies as a democratic socialist but is not a member of the D.S.A., with which he has some disagreements. “It was just so low-brow and unfunny. It can’t be the same person who wrote ‘Curb.’”

Many posts focused on Mr. David’s age while criticizing his views, and others described him as unfunny and racist.

“Maybe I’m just too young, but who is Larry David and why would any person alive care what he has to say?” said a user who identified themselves as DSA_Girly.

The Times sought to confirm the identities of the users who wrote these posts, but some declined to be interviewed or did not immediately respond to interview requests.

Mr. David, whose comedy has made him a millionaire many times over, did not mock the D.S.A.’s economic proposals, which include universal health care, raising the minimum wage and expanding public housing and child care. The movement’s focus on economic inequality is central to its appeal for many voters, who are struggling with higher costs and a dismal view of their financial future.

Mr. David seemed to anticipate the backlash his piece would provoke, daring his socialist targets to take the joke.

His last proposal mandates that any comedian who causes “emotional discomfort” be sent to be “re-programmed” to emerge with greater sensitivity.

And if that effort fails, Mr. David offers one final “modest” suggestion: “The repeat offender will be sent to Pitcairn Island to live with the Bagel People.”

item.title: The Frenzy Behind Getting an Initiative on the California Ballot
item.description:
Dederek Huff scanned the grassy hillside of Dolores Park in San Francisco one day this spring and saw dozens of people relaxing on picnic blankets and park benches.

To most people, it was an idyllic scene on a sunny day. To Mr. Huff, however, it was an opportunity to earn as much as $125 from each person in the park who would sign the stack of petitions under his arm.

“How y’all doing?” Mr. Huff asked as he approached a group of friends on a blanket. “Are you registered to vote?”

With his ease talking to strangers and his knack for reading a crowd, Mr. Huff used the same skills he said he had developed in a very different setting: selling party drugs on the Las Vegas Strip.

He had come to San Francisco because word had spread that campaigns were paying big money to place measures on the November ballot. So much, in fact, that Mr. Huff said he found he could make more money dealing democracy than dope.

“This is better than drug money,” said Mr. Huff, who has had drug-related arrests in Nevada, records show.

Mr. Huff was part of a small army of petition circulators who fanned out to shopping centers and street corners this spring, becoming the main reason that the ballots sent to California voters this month are stuffed with statewide initiatives.

California’s direct democracy system began over a century ago as a populist reform meant to empower citizens and bypass the special interests that controlled the State Legislature. Over the years, though, ballot measures have morphed into a sprawling industry fueled by moneyed interests that spend whatever it takes to put their ideas before voters.

This year, campaigns had to collect nearly 900,000 valid signatures to qualify a measure for the November ballot. To hit that number, most initiative efforts had to hire companies that specialize in this slice of the political process. The firms, in turn, contracted with smaller companies that paid people like Mr. Huff for each verified signature.

A flurry of spending was set off in January when a health care workers union began circulating petitions to put the billionaire tax on the ballot. That prompted a coalition of billionaires to flood the marketplace with three countermeasures that could void the tax initiative if they were to receive more votes in November.

Campaigns paid as much as $15 per signature, drawing a raft of enterprising workers — and some alleged fraudsters — to take part in this political underworld. It turned into a bonanza for workers like Mr. Huff, who said he made $43,000 in three months.

“That’s the most money I’ve made in three months of my life,” said Mr. Huff, 38.

All told, California ballot measure campaigns spent $126.5 million on circulating petitions during the first half of the year, four times as much as they spent in the same period in 2024, the last regular election year, according to state campaign finance reports.

As the price per signature doubled in March, a Facebook group for petition circulators lit up with excitement. Commenters called it a legendary season and punctuated their posts with money bag emojis. They shared pictures of invoices for tens of thousands of dollars as they submitted heaps of petitions. Employers recruited circulators from other parts of the country, sometimes offering housing or transportation.

But reports of bad actors and concerns of fraud also permeated the group. Workers posted warnings about managers who didn’t pay them and people who stole signed petitions. Some veteran petitioners expressed fear that the high price for signatures this year was spurring scams.

Things become so frenzied that men in ski masks handed out $5 bills and slices of pizza to people who signed petitions in a San Francisco neighborhood known for drug addiction and homelessness. And last month, three people were criminally charged after they were accused of paying people to sign petitions using stolen identities on Skid Row in Los Angeles.

In one pocket of Southern California, an experienced circulator with the biblical-sounding name of Third Corinthians Walker tried to instill some order. He confronted petition circulators who gave misleading information to voters or offered illegal giveaways. Then he posted their photos on the Facebook group and cited the laws he contended they were violating.

“This was the most hectic season I ever been in, in 25 years,” said Mr. Walker, 46, who lives in Redlands, Calif., about 60 miles east of downtown Los Angeles.

A lot of what he saw fell short of criminal behavior but broke the unspoken code of signature gathering, Mr. Walker said.

There were petitioners who set up tables at 2 a.m. to claim the best spot at a shopping center hours before stores opened. The “turf jumpers” who encroached on spots that other petitioners had already claimed. The “runners” who roamed parking lots and approached people as they got out of their cars.

Mr. Walker grew up in Kansas City, Mo. By the time he was 21, his felony record of gun and drug charges made it difficult to find employment. Feeling desperate, Mr. Walker saw a newspaper ad for a job promising $100 a day and went to an orientation on circulating petitions.

Over time, the work took him to places that he might never have otherwise seen: Florida, Nebraska, Ohio and, eventually, California.

“I felt like it was a blessing from the Lord,” Mr. Walker said.

Now, he runs his petition business with his mother, Melba Walker. They share a home in Southern California where, during the busy season, stacks of petitions covered the coffee table.

Mr. Walker likes the autonomy that comes with his profession, the ability to set his own hours and choose where he spends his time. He said he varies his pitch depending on the politics of the region. When he petitioned in a conservative area this year, he often led with the anti-tax measures; in liberal neighborhoods, he tended to start with the billionaire tax.

Now that it’s the offseason for petitioners, Mr. Walker keeps busy by playing video games and making graphic designs with Christian themes. He is also helping his mother write a book about their experiences as signature gatherers.

In San Francisco, Alex Carpenter, 49, made his first foray into petitioning this year after work dried up on the Northern California cannabis farm where he had spent the last several years.

Signature gathering appealed to Mr. Carpenter’s liberal activist streak, so he set up a table on a bustling corner near Golden Gate Park. It was close to his favorite coffee shop and had a lamppost where he could do pull-ups during lulls in foot traffic. He scrawled “Tax Billionaire$?” on a piece of card stock and taped it to the side of his table.

Many of the petitions on his clipboards represented causes Mr. Carpenter believed in. He liked the proposals to tax billionaires to fund health care, extend a tax hike on high-income earners to fund education and raise sales taxes to fund Bay Area transit. He focused on getting signatures for those initiatives.

He said he was still able to make close to $200 an hour, even though he didn’t actively pursue signatures for the highest compensated proposals that were backed by billionaires. Still, Mr. Carpenter had petitions for those measures on his table, in case voters took the time to get to the bottom of his stack of clipboards.

“I’m trying to make a living,” he said. “I would love to see them make it to the polls and fail.”

Mr. Huff, the petition circulator who sought signatures from voters in Dolores Park, also has strong political views.

He is a conservative and considers himself a part of President Trump’s MAGA movement. He has had an interest in politics ever since he was a teenager growing up in Louisville, Ky., he said.

That didn’t stop him from trying to make as much cash as possible in San Francisco, one of the nation’s most Democratic cities and where Mr. Trump is deeply unpopular.

After he finished gathering signatures this spring, Mr. Huff returned home to Las Vegas, where he spent time with his family for several weeks and used some of his petition money to buy new furniture and get work done on his teeth.

Despite his conservative views, Mr. Huff said he would do petition work for any campaign that pays him. So when a friend offered him a job gathering signatures for liberal-backed initiatives in Colorado this summer, Mr. Huff packed his bags and went.

Then he heard that conservative interest groups were also paying for signatures in Colorado.

“‘Well, bro,’ I said, ‘You got to get me on both petitions,’” Mr. Huff recalled.

“If I’m going to Colorado, I need as much petitions in my hand as possible because, of course, I’m trying to make the most money.”

Jill Cowan contributed reporting from Los Angeles. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: At a Last-Hope Health Clinic, Desperation, Kindness and Fear for What’s Next
item.description:
The early morning caller to Dr. Sarah Hershman’s personal cellphone was a patient.

Dr. Hershman, who works at a public health clinic in Nampa, Idaho, isn’t supposed to give out her private number. But she has been sharing it with some patients who she knows have no other recourse, telling them, “You really need to be able to contact me.”

Sophia Perez, 28, whose family has no health insurance, spoke in a frightened voice. Her husband, John, had been welding, she told Dr. Hershman, when he felt a hot sting on his eyeball. Could it have been hit by a metal shard? They could not afford a visit to a hospital emergency room.

Dr. Hershman asked careful questions and slipped him into the clinic’s packed Saturday roster.

Full Circle Health, where Dr. Hershman practices family medicine, has long been a last-hope safety net in the American health system. It is one of 1,400 networks known as federally qualified health centers with thousands of sites that receive federal funds to care for patients regardless of their ability to pay.

Now their caseloads are growing, even as revenues are falling. With cuts to Medicaid mounting and the cost of Obamacare insurance plans soaring, the clinic’s doctors and counselors are going to new lengths to patch together care for people with complex medical issues who are underinsured and uninsured.

Dr. Hershman and her colleagues have been spending hours providing unpaid care, emailing advice, calling after hours. They forage for cheaper but sometimes less effective medicines and spend weeks adjusting doses to make them as effective as possible. They negotiate with specialists to accept patients and offer to perform the work-up exams and follow-ups themselves.

Idaho has been one of the most aggressive states to slash Medicaid rolls over the past few years, affecting patients as well as clinics like Full Circle’s, which rely heavily on those funds to stay solvent. Now pressures on patients as well as clinics are about to become even worse, not only in the state but also throughout the country.

As harvest season for sugar beets, onions and potatoes winds down here, two ominous events loom on the calendar.

The annual enrollment period for Your Health Idaho, the state’s Obamacare marketplace, began on Oct. 15, but the generous government subsidies that helped make plans affordable are no longer available because Congress declined to renew them. Like many people, Mrs. Perez, whose job at an orthodontist practice includes filing insurance claims for patients yet cannot wrangle health care for her husband and 2-year-old, found that even the cheapest plan was out of reach. “It was all so overwhelming,” she said with tears in her eyes during her half-hour lunch break.

And come January, many patients covered by Medicaid — whose incomes are well under the state’s limits — may lose coverage. On New Year’s Day, new work requirements for eligibility, enacted as part of President Trump’s sweeping domestic policy bill, begin across the country. Idaho’s rules are among the nation’s most stringent.

At 8 a.m., Debbie Lehnert, a community health worker at the clinic, replenished a filing cabinet drawer with patient stress busters for the day: Bubble wrap for popping and Little Debbie Swiss rolls, the primal ones with chocolate cake, cream filling and fudge coating.

Ms. Lehnert’s responsibilities include connecting distressed patients with emergency health coverage and support services.

For weeks, she and her peers in public health clinics across the state have been under a weighty new burden: The rapidly approaching Medicaid work rules. Community health workers have been convening regularly in videoconferences to puzzle through the rules, discussing patient hypotheticals that none of them can answer with certainty.

Starting in January, Idaho patients will have to show documentation that they have worked or volunteered at least 80 hours a month for the previous three months. (Most states will require one month.) Reauthorization for the program will double in frequency, from the traditional yearly review to every six months. The requirements are expected to eventually reduce Medicaid rolls nationwide by five million people, the Congressional Budget Office estimates.

One of Ms. Lehnert’s most urgent tasks right now is to alert patients. She dialed the next one on her bottomless list. The young man, who can’t get his diabetes under control, had qualified for Medicaid after he lost his job at the post office for using too many sick days. Now his reauthorization date coincides with the start of the new work rules.

“I just wanted to see where you are in that process, if there’s anything I can do to help with that?” Ms. Lehnert said, gently prodding. “January is just around the corner.”

Given the man’s bleak health, it is unlikely he will be able to produce three pay stubs in time. Ms. Lehnert said that with the clinic’s records about his chronic diabetes, they could collaborate to seek an initial medical exemption.

“My hope is that would give you time to focus on getting better and finding employment, so that the second determination in six months would be easier,” she said.

“OK, yeah,” he replied dully.

Ms. Lehnert suggested they meet to attack the paperwork together. Or do a three-way call with a state assistant. Or he could file online, where, studies show, procedural errors, such as computer mistakes and confusion over directions, are the biggest reasons for lost coverage.

“OK, yeah,” he said.

“So which would you like to choose?” she pressed.

He chose online.

After they hung up, Ms. Lehnert buried her head in her hands.

“I truly feel like this is a calling, and I won’t do anything else,” she said, giving her dark curls an emphatic shake. “But these days, I’ve never hated doing my job more.”

It was just after 6 p.m. on a Thursday, but the buzzy restaurant was already slammed with people waiting for tables. Amid the kitchen chaos, Oscar Casarez, 37, a line cook and a patient at the Nampa clinic, kept his head down, juggling grill times and rhythmically seasoning burgers, steaks and salmon.

Just over a year ago, Mr. Casarez, lightheaded and gasping, drove himself to a hospital in septic shock. He was placed in a medically induced coma. By the time he was discharged nearly four weeks later, his employer had replaced him, leaving him uninsured as well as unemployed.

To cover Mr. Casarez’s six-figure bill, the hospital helped him get emergency Medicaid, which carried him through countless clinic visits, scans, blood transfusions and medications as well as hospital stays each time his newly diagnosed severe ulcerative colitis flared up.

Yet he managed to secure line-cook shifts. In May, he was booted off Medicaid because he started earning too much.

He works at two restaurants; neither offers health insurance. But his health problems continue: He also has a blood clot in his liver.

To help, Dr. Amanda Aman, his primary care doctor at the Nampa clinic, has been coordinating with a local gastroenterologist so she can monitor him at the clinic for lower fees than the specialist would charge. Case managers at the clinic scrounged for less expensive medication. After determining that the only drug that quells his colitis attacks requires an out-of-pocket monthly cost of more than $14,000, they helped enroll him in a special program that will provide the drug free for a year.

Still, given his precarious health, Mr. Casarez knows he needs insurance. His only option is to buy a plan on the state’s Obamacare marketplace.

He will likely have to select the most bare-bones policy, which has monthly premiums of about $310 and a deductible of $10,000. The plan doesn’t even cover his gastroenterologist.

At most, when he works 10 straight days of double shifts (to get an entire weekend with his 9-year-old son), Mr. Casarez can earn $3,800 a month. Rent takes a $1,400 chunk; then there are utilities, car payments, gas, child support, food, toiletries.

It comes down to this, he said: He can pay bills and insurance by working overtime at two jobs, almost guaranteeing a slow, steady death march. Or he can work fewer hours and get on Medicaid but have no money for housing and bills.

“I feel like I’m damned if I do and damned if I don’t,” he said.

Late one afternoon, Dr. Ty Waters, the tattooed director of Full Circle’s Nampa South clinic, unfurled himself into a chair in Ms. Lehnert’s office. He mused sarcastically about getting teardrops tattooed down one cheekbone, prison gang style, to signal the fights he gets into on behalf of his patients. He would nickname the tattoos his “Medicaid tears.”

Recently, a manual laborer without insurance injured his leg but held off coming in for weeks, wary of racking up a flurry of the clinic’s income-adjusted fees. When at last he limped in, Dr. Waters, who suspected that the man had torn his anterior cruciate ligament, treated him free of charge, put him in a stabilizing brace so he could return to work and coordinated with an orthopedist who would see him without requiring an expensive M.R.I.

“Our patients are basically people who are already struggling, who lose coverage and then get penalized for asking for help,” Dr. Waters said.

Dr. Hershman, who teaches family medicine to residents at the clinic, poked her head into Ms. Lehnert’s office, rubbing her face wearily. Every week, she allows a battered woman to sit in a clinic room for as long as she needs because the woman feels safe there. Dr. Hershman bills only a few dollars for the visit. It’s hardly conventional health care, she said, “but it’s that nexus of what we can do to improve their social situation and, therefore, their health outcomes.”

Her eyes glistened. “I love my patients, and I want to show up every day and be the person that they need,” she said. “Because even though this job is hard, being them is so, so much harder.”

(Dr. Hershman knows personally what it’s like to face crushing medical debt: After being treated for cancer recently, she discovered that her insurance doesn’t cover fertility preservation procedures. In addition, she owes $450,000 for her medical education.)

Too many times, Dr. Hershman said, she has sat with deathly ill patients who are nonetheless consumed with worries about cost, anxious about burdening their survivors with medical bills.

She treated a 59-year-old tech writer with a chronic gastrointestinal bleed that had turned life-threatening: Normal hemoglobin levels for men range between 13.5 and 17.5; his was 3.5. Or, as she put it: “He literally had no blood in the tank. I don’t know how his brain was functioning.”

She felt strongly that he needed to be hospitalized in intensive care because he required emergency surgery and, likely, a stay of five days. Chatting him up about his adored grandbaby, she almost got him to agree.

But then he dug in and, however reluctantly, refused. Her notes from that visit read: “Pt. doesn’t want to be here because of financial situation. Working to get insurance with open enrollment but has limited means.”

item.title: Ken Paxton Has Tried to Overturn Tight Elections. He’s in One of His Own.
item.description:
In the immediate aftermath of the 2020 election, President Trump’s allies searched for a Republican state attorney general willing to back a last-ditch legal effort to challenge the results.

They found their man in Texas: Ken Paxton.

“No one had the courage or the clarity of legal understanding to do it,” Aaron Reitz, a top deputy to Mr. Paxton at the time, said in an interview. “Paxton and I were adamant that something needed to be done.”

The suit quickly failed at the U.S. Supreme Court, which found Texas had no standing to try to invalidate votes cast in another state. But it firmly established Mr. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, as a partisan fighter willing to wield the power of his office to aid Republicans, attack Democrats and challenge election results. It made him a conservative star and helped him secure Mr. Trump’s critical endorsement, propelling Mr. Paxton forward as the party’s nominee this year for U.S. Senate in Texas.

Early voting starts on Monday.

Since 2020, Mr. Paxton has continued to use his office to intervene in election disputes and pursue political opponents. Mr. Paxton has sued the former congressman Beto O’Rourke, tried to shut down a Latino voter registration group, opposed the counting of provisional ballots in Houston and unsuccessfully tried to criminally indict a sitting county election administrator.

Now, as he is locked in an extremely close contest against James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, Mr. Paxton’s record of election-related legal challenges and partisan legal actions has raised the question of how he would respond, in his capacity as attorney general and as a candidate, if he were to lose in November.

The Texas Senate race appears to have all the makings for a potential post-election legal fight by Mr. Paxton, should he lose. The contest is especially important to Republicans, who risk losing a statewide race for the first time in three decades and whose control of the U.S. Senate could hinge on the outcome. Current polls show Mr. Talarico with an edge in a tightening race.

“We have to win,” Mr. Paxton said at a rally hosted by President Trump in San Antonio this month.

Mr. Paxton, now in his third term as attorney general, has pushed to expand the powers of his office to prosecute criminal violations of Texas election law. Those efforts led to a clash with the state’s highest criminal court, made up of all Republican judges, which ruled that he lacked the authority under the state Constitution to independently prosecute election crimes.

After that loss, Mr. Paxton campaigned against the judges who ruled against him and were up for re-election, helping to oust them in a Republican primary in 2024. The next year, Republicans in the Texas Legislature passed a new law, Senate Bill 12, granting Mr. Paxton the authority to prosecute election crimes. But he has yet to test its constitutionality, and legal experts have said courts may again stymie Mr. Paxton if he tries.

His campaign defended his record.

“Ken Paxton has never apologized for enforcing Texas election law, and he never will,” Mr. Paxton’s campaign spokeswoman, Madison Cercy, said. “When elections are run fairly and the law is followed, every Texan wins.”

The attorney general’s office could also play a role, post-election, in investigating allegations of criminal conduct, or in securing election materials if asked by the secretary of state, who was appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican. The examination of the election materials would be directed by a state court.

Elections experts and voting security advocates said they worried that election challenges could be made in Texas, but they did not believe such challenges would be effective.

“The power he has under Texas law to enforce those criminal laws is quite limited,” said David Froomkin, a law professor at the University of Houston.

David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research in Washington, D.C., said that while the election could “potentially be a very volatile situation,” he was confident the courts and election officials in Texas were “going to hold firm.”

Mr. Abbott is tasked with certifying election results under state law, except in his own race and the lieutenant governor’s race, when the final canvass is done by the Legislature.

The role of the governor and Legislature in this process is ceremonial, election experts said, though he or the Legislature could face pressure to delay certification. This year, Mr. Abbott named Nate Schatzline, a hard-right former state representative who has questioned the 2020 election results, to be a senior adviser on elections.

Election challenges are permitted under Texas law. But Texas Republicans have, in recent years, challenged election results even when the outcome appeared clear.

In Harris County, which includes Houston, Republicans contested losses in more than a dozen races in 2022 — including one that the Democrat won by 15 points. Republicans cited what they said were problems at the polls. A court ordered a new election in only one case, a local judicial race.

Mr. Paxton also intervened on Election Day in 2022 to stop the counting of provisional ballots cast at locations in Harris County that had been kept open an extra hour. He sought to have the votes discarded. The Texas Supreme Court ruled against Mr. Paxton, ordering them to be counted — but left the possibility of further litigation open should the ballots cast during the extended voting hour swing any results. (They didn’t.)

Even within his own office, Mr. Paxton’s 2020 election challenge in support of Mr. Trump appeared to be contentious.

The solicitor general at the time, Kyle Hawkins, did not sign the Supreme Court filing, which Mr. Paxton signed himself along with Kurt Olsen, a lawyer who helped craft the unusual lawsuit that tried to challenge the election.

“Ken Paxton showed a tremendous amount of courage to take this on,” Mr. Olsen said in an interview this month.

Mr. Paxton, along with Mr. Reitz, his deputy for legal strategy, then brought the case to other Republican attorneys general to get them to file a supporting brief, Mr. Reitz said in the interview. Seventeen attorneys general signed on.

“It was a moment of character-revealing pressure,” Mr. Reitz said.

The Supreme Court quickly turned them all down.

Still, Mr. Paxton stood by his election challenge at a rally with Mr. Trump in Washington on Jan. 6, 2021. “If you look at what Georgia did, they capitulated, they consented,” Mr. Paxton told the crowd, referring to the state’s rapid certifications of its results. “We kept fighting in Texas.”

Mr. Olsen, who previously served as an elections czar for the White House, now works for the Justice Department. He recently stepped down from a high-profile elections investigation.

Mr. Reitz is now the top federal prosecutor in the Southern District of Texas, which includes Houston. He said in the interview that he would “muster all of my legal and law enforcement troops to ensure that federal law is upheld” in the 2026 election. But, he added, elections are primarily a state matter.

Since 2020, Mr. Paxton has announced dozens of election-related actions, including investigations and lawsuits.

Mr. Paxton tried in 2021 to prosecute Dana DeBeauvoir, who ran elections in Travis County, which includes Austin, on a charge of obstructing a poll observer in violation of Texas law. A grand jury declined to indict. In an interview, Ms. DeBeauvoir urged vigilance. “We’re at high alert,” she said. She added, “Let’s not let scare tactics work.”

In 2024, Mr. Paxton opened an investigation into Jolt Initiative, claiming the organization, which focuses on registering young Latino voters, had been illegally registering unauthorized migrants. The group sued, and a federal judge in Austin blocked his investigation, ruling the attorney general had acted in “bad faith.”

“Defendant could not offer any plausible proof,” the judge, Robert Pitman, wrote.

The suit had a significant financial impact, said Jackie Bastard, Jolt’s executive director, forcing it to cut its staff to five people from 35. The group has been able to register voters this year, Ms. Bastard said, but not at the same scale.

Then last fall, Mr. Paxton sued Mr. O’Rourke, the former Democratic congressman, and his voter registration group, claiming potential fund-raising violations. An all-Republican appeals court sided with Mr. O’Rourke. (The Texas Supreme Court, whose nine members are also all Republicans, declined to intervene.)

But as with Jolt, the case cost Mr. O’Rourke’s group time and more than $400,000, and, had it continued, could have bankrupted the organization, Mr. O’Rourke said at the time.

“We have seen Paxton try to use the power of the office to promote his political goals and the goals of his allies,” said Mimi Marziani, a lawyer and the former president of the Texas Civil Rights Project who represented Mr. O’Rourke.

“What I will say, which gives me a lot of hope,” she added, “is that by and large he has not been successful in the courts.”

A dispute over the election could end up before the Texas Supreme Court. The court’s newest member is Mr. Hawkins, the former solicitor general who did not sign on to Mr. Paxton’s election challenge in 2020.

item.title: Republicans in Ohio Are Worried About Turnout. Here’s What They’re Doing About it.
item.description:
Just two volunteers showed up on a recent weekday at a Republican Party campaign office near Cleveland that in 2024 was brimming with activity every night.

One of the two, Tanya Karabanovs, 54, sat among stacks of untouched yard signs and brainstormed new ways to convince her neighbors to vote for Republican candidates such as Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed in 2025 to finish the term of Vice President JD Vance. Her most recent idea: stuffing chocolate bars into goodie bags with leftover campaign literature.

“This is really a weird cycle,” said Ms. Karabanovs, who recalled at least 30 volunteers packing into the office each day in 2024. “There’s no way to feel confident about any of the races, honestly.”

Many of the Republican volunteers trying to keep Ohio’s Senate seat red started the summer making the case that, despite rising prices, Mr. Husted was better suited to fix the economy than his Democratic challenger, the former senator Sherrod Brown. But when it became clear that the message wasn’t landing, they began to pivot.

Some, like Ms. Karabanovs, got creative. The political PAC for Americans for Prosperity, a prominent conservative advocacy group that deploys thousands of door-knockers across the state, switched its script to the threat of socialism — and organizers quickly noticed a difference.

“I wouldn’t like that,” said Nikki Cvetkovic, 77, after opening her door in a working-class suburb of Youngstown and inspecting a pamphlet with a picture of Brown next to the words, “SOCIALISM THREATENS YOUR FREEDOM.” She said she would cast her ballot for Mr. Husted.

Polls have shown Mr. Brown running ahead of Mr. Husted in one of the most closely watched races of this cycle. But many conservatives across the state believe they can pull off in the final two weeks what Republicans have done better than Democrats for the last 10 years: defy expectations on Election Day.

The modern-day Republican Party is built on upsets. Twice, polls showed Mr. Trump losing the presidential election only for him to triumph, cementing the MAGA movement’s staying power and underdog status. The question now is whether the G.O.P. can do it again, at a time when Mr. Trump is not on the ballot and his popularity is historically low.

The answer lies on the ground in unexpected battlegrounds, including Iowa and Ohio, which have swung to the right over the last decade but this year have shown signs of shifting back. In these states, as the Republican Party has struggled to defend Mr. Trump’s handling of inflation, the war with Iran and tariff policies, local campaigns and committees have leaned into depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left — a last-ditch gambit to persuade their voters not to stay home or break the other way.

In a historically expensive midterm cycle, the Republican Party apparatus has poured more money into Ohio’s Senate race than all but one other contest, spending more than $277 million as of Saturday, according to AdImpact. At least a third of that spending has gone toward negative advertisements about Mr. Brown, many of which depict him as part of the far-left wing of the Democratic Party.

At Mr. Trump’s rally in Youngstown on Monday, he called Mr. Brown the “candidate of the Marxists, the communists, the anti-American radicals who want to tear down America’s heritage.”

It may not be enough. Representative Max Miller, one of President Trump’s closest allies in the House who has been besieged by allegations of domestic violence against his young daughter and ex-wife, came out against the war in Iran on Wednesday night during a meet-and-greet at a pub in Parma, a union town south of Cleveland.

National Republicans have withdrawn campaign funds from Ohio’s First Congressional District, where they had hoped to unseat a Democrat.

And a Republican National Committee operative circulated an email this week with data from Ohio showing Democrats outperforming Republicans in early vote, absentee votes and ballot requests compared with 2022 and 2018, according to an email reviewed by The Times.

Democrats in Ohio remain optimistic about returning Mr. Brown to the Senate, mostly because of Mr. Trump’s low approval rating and the deteriorating economy. But they also have benefited from Mr. Husted’s struggle to introduce himself to voters since he took office 21 months ago.

A former lieutenant governor and member of the House known for his outward reserve, Mr. Husted has tethered himself for much of the year to Mr. Trump, but he has also spent significant time describing his biography, including his time as a college football player and his upbringing as the son of a local factory worker focused on bringing jobs to the state.

Republicans, including Mr. Husted, are bracing for narrow margins on Election Day.

“We have a tough race, there is no doubt about that,” Mr. Husted said at an event last week at a G.O.P. field office in Mahoning County, which sprawls across three units of a strip mall in a region that once powered the country’s steel industry. “Midterm elections are tough.”

Mr. Husted had drawn a full house to the outpost in the Youngstown area, with supporters crammed between a plaque celebrating the Second Amendment and boxes of pizza. The crowd cheered when he took the lectern. As he spoke, rows of people nodded along and held up their phones to snap pictures.

“Find someone you haven’t talked to in a while, call them,” Mr. Husted continued. “You tell them I told you to call and ask them to vote, tell them that you spent time with me.”

Sitting in a plastic chair and listening along was Doris Layfield, who works at the board of elections in Mahoning County. She said she had knocked on doors for Mr. Husted and that she had liked what he said in person.

“Honestly, it’s really kind of scary,” she said. “If he doesn’t win, I really do feel like we will be living under communist rule.”

Mr. Brown, who was defeated in 2024 after three terms in the Senate, lost Mahoning County for the first time that year. The margin was just 220 votes.

He is aware that his victory is far from assured in a state that Mr. Trump won by 11 percentage points the same year he was unseated. He also seems to know that Republican claims that he’s a radical could resonate among Ohio’s increasingly conservative voters. He cut one ad, for instance, that responded to attacks from his opponent and an Elon Musk-backed PAC regarding transgender issues.

Mostly, though, Mr. Brown is running on the same progressive populism that has defined his political career since the 1970s.

In speeches at union halls, Mr. Brown talks about how the economy is “rigged,” says Congress is controlled by insider trading and describes Mr. Husted as a “special interest guy in Washington” who is detached from working-class people. He has also targeted Mr. Husted for his support for investments in data centers while he served in state government.

Aware of the resonance of the issue in Ohio, Mr. Husted sponsored a bill that passed in the House last month that encourages states to make data centers pay for higher energy costs, though it would not compel them to do so.

Back in the Youngstown area, Donovan O’Neil, a senior adviser in Ohio for Americans for Prosperity’s political PAC, walked up to a house with an American flag hanging from its porch. Barb Delaney, 65, a part-time bookkeeper, answered.

“Are you planning to vote?” Mr. O’Neil asked.

“Oh hell yes,” said Ms. Delaney, who was wearing a Detroit Lions T-shirt. “For Sherrod.”

Mr. O’Neil was not ready to walk away. He said he’d like to ask Ms. Delaney, a self-identified Democrat, a follow-up question: “Are there concerns for you with the rise of socialism, the Democrat Socialists of America?”

There were some, she said. But Ms. Delaney was far more incensed this year about data centers, and she blamed Mr. Husted. Because of a nearby development, she said, her energy bill, which includes heat for her pool, had surged from $200 a month to almost $500 — by far the highest it had been in the 28 years she had lived in her current home.

“My electric bill is skyrocketing,” she said. “Nobody wants data centers around.”

Then, referring to Mr. Husted, she added: “I will not vote for that man. I would never.”

Mr. O’Neil listened, and after a few more attempts to engage her, he continued down the block.

item.title: Who’s Winning the Race for Congress?
item.description:
It’s triage season.

With just over two weeks to go until the midterm elections, Republicans reeling in a sour national environment have begun pulling spending out of tough territory, essentially cutting their losses in some races in an effort to rescue others.

North Carolina appears to be out. Kansas is in. Some House incumbents in New Jersey and Iowa are now on their own, while others in places like Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are receiving fresh infusions of national cash.

But even as the battleground moves into redder territory, Republicans see some signs of hope.

Polls are tightening in three Senate races in which Democrats have enjoyed narrow but consistent polling leads: Texas, Ohio and Michigan. And, thanks to a cascade of outside money, Republicans have ample resources to keep hammering their opponents in those states and beyond. Still, Democrats believe that momentum and time are on their side.

On Oct. 1, Brent Robertson, the chief of staff for Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, told other Republican chiefs of staff at a private lunch in Washington that Mr. Marshall’s team had things under control in his unexpectedly tight re-election fight, according to a person in the room, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private discussion. In 10 days’ time, he promised, Kansas wouldn’t be a problem. (Robertson did not respond to requests for comment.)

That is not how things have panned out. Kansas remains squarely part of the unusually large map of tossup races. Republicans’ main super PAC has now spent or reserved more than $11.6 million shoring up Marshall, who has struggled with fund-raising in the face of a stiff challenge from Adam Hamilton, a Democratic pastor.

Those tossups still include other red states such as Alaska and Iowa. Republican groups have also spent millions in Nebraska and South Carolina in an effort to stave off any more surprising momentum from their opponents in two more states President Trump has won handily.

But none of this means Democrats are breathing easily. Their candidates have failed to open commanding polling leads in several states that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024, including Maine, Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire.

Another week, another set of House races shifted by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report toward Democrats. This time, it was 11 races, more than half of which are in the Midwest.

Democrats are moving ahead with plans to spend money in ever-redder battlegrounds, including House districts in states such as Colorado, South Carolina and Texas. In those districts, voters heavily favored Trump in 2024.

Republicans are sending resources to help incumbents such as Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Bryan Steil of Wisconsin.

They are also pulling back from some of their offensive plays. The Congressional Leadership Fund and a political action committee aligned with Trump’s operation have both paused their ad spending in the district held by Representative Tom Suozzi, a Long Island Democrat, according to data from the media tracking firm AdImpact.

Republicans have a significant advantage in midterm spending, powered by their reliance on big donors and outside groups. That’s allowed them to spend more than $300 million more than Democrats on the Senate races that could determine control of the chamber.

But the party’s advantage is a lot narrower when it comes to House races.

Sources: Cook Political Report; New York Times analysis of AdImpact data.

Jillian Vordick and Lazaro Gamio/The New York Times

That might be an indication of both parties’ belief that it’s increasingly unlikely that Republicans will be able to hold their narrow House majority. Donors want to shape the contest that’s widely seen as up in the air — and that’s the race for control of the Senate.

There’s been lots of attention paid to the Senate race in Texas, where Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, has funneled $158 million to prop up the scandal-prone state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

But it’s actually Ohio that could be the most expensive Senate general election race of the midterms, according to AdImpact, with more than $420 million in total spending.

For the upcoming week alone, Republicans have reserved nearly $23 million in ads supporting Senator Jon Husted. Former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, has nearly $11.5 million booked.

The race appears to be a top priority for Trump, who has rallied twice in the state this month. He also held a rally in Northern Kentucky — which is part of the Cincinnati media market — over the weekend.

3.7 percent: That’s how much higher prices were in September, compared with a year earlier.

The rising inflation is largely because of soaring energy prices, which have been pushed up by the war in Iran.

It was a messy week in Washington: A brand-new press secretary fired after five days. An ambassador ousted after she was accused of shaking down a donor. A key Trump ally accused of misallocating donations for the Kennedy Center.

None of that has anything to do with the midterms, directly. But it all amounts to a distraction from the Trump administration’s efforts to show that it is focused on getting the economy back on track.

48 percent.

That’s the share of Americans who say they are financially worse off since Trump returned to office, according to a poll by The Washington Post, ABC News and Ipsos. That, The Post reported, is the highest that figure has been since 1986.

An unexpected Republican senator broke with Trump last week: Darline Graham of South Carolina.

Graham is campaigning for a full term in the seat that her brother, Lindsey Graham, held for decades before he suddenly died in July, and she’s been deeply reliant on the support of the president.

But on Saturday, she gently criticized Trump for exempting Russia from a sanctions measure named after her brother.

“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” Graham told reporters at a campaign event. “Because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.”

“Oh, shut up.”

That was Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Maine, during his fourth and final debate with Senator Susan Collins, a Republican. Mr. Jackson’s words came after Ms. Collins accused him of coordinating with a protester who had begun yelling in the audience.

Ms. Collins has since suggested the remark was indicative of how Mr. Jackson treats women. In an interview on Sunday, Mr. Jackson stuck by his words.

“I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me,” he said in a Sunday interview on CNN. “And so I’m not — I’m not going to apologize for that now.”

item.title: Vital Early Voting Period Begins in Texas
item.description:
The time has finally come: Texans can begin casting ballots on Monday, and their early votes will help determine whether a prospective Democratic revival nationwide will upend three decades of statewide Republican rule.

Most votes in Texas tend to be cast early, with 80 percent coming before Election Day in 2024 and about two-thirds in 2022, according to state election data. That means campaigns will be hustling to get their supporters to the polls from now until Oct. 30, when the state’s early voting period ends.

The candidates in the Senate race — Ken Paxton, the Republican, and James Talarico, the Democrat — have already begun statewide tours, and will be holding events around the state almost daily through Election Day.

On Monday night, the candidates are set to hold dueling rallies in Fort Worth, underscoring the importance of the city and surrounding Tarrant County. Mr. Paxton and his Republican supporters are looking to mobilize their voters in an area of the state where Democrats have been making inroads recently, while Mr. Talarico and his party see the county, a swingy area in recent elections, as crucial to any statewide victory.

But by now both candidate’s faces and voices have been seared into the eyes (and ears) of Texas, thanks to the more than half a billion dollars that have been spent on television advertising already. Much of the spending has come late in the race, and a huge portion of it has been financed by one man, Elon Musk, to benefit one candidate, Mr. Paxton.

Both Senate candidates are coming off rocky periods in their campaigns. Mr. Talarico was absent from the campaign trail for nine days because of what he has said was a “nasty case of the flu.” Mr. Paxton has faced a run of unflattering headlines, including one after a video showed him celebrating New Year’s Eve in 2024 at a Dubai high-rise with two fugitives and a woman who is not his wife — months before their divorce was announced publicly.

The Senate race isn’t the only hotly contested campaign on the ballot. Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, is hoping that he can win a record fourth term. But polls have shown that even Mr. Abbott — a prodigious fund-raiser and able campaigner — has been struggling amid the general sour mood of the electorate.

Unlike in previous races, Mr. Abbott has opted not to debate his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, an Austin state representative. Mr. Abbott agreed, in 2022, to a televised debate against Beto O’Rourke, a much better known opponent. (Mr. Abbott won that race by double digits.)

But the governor’s decision was in keeping with that of other Republicans in statewide races this year: None have agreed to debate their Democratic opponents. Some odd moments have resulted, like Mr. Talarico’s appearance at a CNN town hall, debating with Republican voters who are not Mr. Paxton, or Ms. Hinojosa’s staging a debate against an empty lectern in front of the governor’s mansion in Austin.

It once seemed as though the one debate that would take place would be between candidates for the statewide position of railroad commissioner, which helps regulate the oil and gas industry. The race has attracted lots of attention this year, after the hard-right anti-immigration Republican candidate, Bo French, posted racist attacks after seeing South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game. He had been slated to debate Jon Rosenthal, the Democrat, but said last week that the showdown would not happen.

item.title: That Huge Republican Cash Edge? It’s in Senate Races, Not House Races.
item.description:
Republicans have an enormous financial edge in this year’s midterms. But with two weeks until the election, it is now clear that their spending advantage is overwhelmingly playing out only in the advertising battle for the Senate — not the House.

In the seven Senate races that the Cook Political Report rated as tossups, Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by $947 million to $625 million. That is a breathtaking advantage of more than $320 million in the key races that could determine which party wins control of the Senate, according to a tally by AdImpact of ads that have been already been shown and future reservations.

It is a very different story in the House, though. Republicans still have an advertising advantage in the closest House races, but it is relatively narrow — just a $14 million edge across the 21 races rated as tossups.

There are a number of explanations for the discrepancy.

Senate races generally attract more money and attention than congressional contests. Elon Musk’s enormous spending on the Texas Senate race is also a factor: He gave nearly $170 million to super PACs backing Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee there — a huge injection of cash from one person.

But it is also appears to be an indication that both parties — and their donors — are viewing it as increasingly unlikely that Republicans will be able to hold onto their House majority. The battle to win control of the Senate, though, remains on a knife’s edge. Republican donors are accordingly spending big in key Senate races.

In six of the seven tossup Senate races, Republican ad spending is far outstripping Democrats’. The biggest gap is in Texas ($141 million), but there are chasms also in Ohio (nearly $90 million), Maine (nearly $32 million) and Michigan ($33 million).

Only in Kansas — where Republicans are engaged in a late rescue mission — is the spending even close. There, Democrats had an edge of less than $2 million.

In the House, there is not such a clear-cut edge for Republicans. Across the 21 tossup districts, Republicans are currently set to spend more on 10 seats while Democrats are set to spend more on 11.

It is worth noting that in recent years, Democrats have lapped Republicans in House spending. In President Trump’s first midterm election, in 2018, G.O.P. strategists spoke about being washed away in a “green wave” as much as a blue one.

“This cycle, that money won’t save them,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee. “Republicans have the money, the map and the message.”

Republicans do have a roughly $30 million spending edge in the dozen seats that are leaning Democratic — but Democrats have a narrow edge of less than $1 million in the 13 seats that are currently rated as leaning Republican.

By Cook Political Report rating.

Note: Figures are rounded. Data as of Sunday, Oct. 18 at 10 a.m.

Sources: Cook Political Report; New York Times analysis of AdImpact data.

The New York Times

“We came into this cycle preparing for the worst-case scenario in Republican spending, and planned accordingly,” said CJ Warnke, a spokesman for the House Majority PAC, the biggest super PAC for House Democrats. “While we’re fighting deep into Trump territory, the G.O.P. spending advantage will ultimately leave some winnable seats on the table.”

These ratings are fluid. Cook has moved numerous races into the Democratic direction in recent weeks.

Dollars spent do not directly equal ads aired. Candidates are entitled to cheaper TV rates than super PACs are under federal law. Democrats are generally spending more on ads at that cheaper rate because Democratic candidates for both the House and the Senate are raising far more than Republican candidates. Republican groups, though, have a big advantage over Democratic ones, led by Mr. Trump’s allied super PACs and Mr. Musk’s wallet.

Every major Senate Democratic candidate is crushing their Republican counterparts in fund-raising.

item.title: Latest Climate Report Warns of Major Upheaval to California Way of Life
item.description:
In just a few decades, summers in California will not only be much hotter, but will also stretch for months longer. Floods will become more widespread and extreme. Exposure to wildfire smoke will kill thousands more people every year.

Those are the dire projections of California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment, a report produced by California every few years that analyzes the impacts of changing weather patterns on the nation’s most-populous state.

The future laid out in the report, which was published on Monday, touches on familiar warnings: more wildfires, bigger storms, longer droughts. But it illustrates in unsettling detail just how quickly the climate is being reshaped, and reveals what is likely to be major upheaval to long-established ways of life in California.

According to the report, average temperatures are likely to increase in California by about 4 degrees Fahrenheit by the middle of the century, and by 5 to 8 degrees by 2100. Current warming in California is unprecedented compared with the past century and estimates for the past millennium, the report shows.

More and more, warm weather will arrive in California earlier in the year and persist later, with summer conditions lasting for 135 days on average by the middle of the century, compared with an average of 90 days between 1981 and 2010, according to the report. That prolonged summer will have widespread impacts, including on fire risk, tourism, agriculture and wildlife.

The warmer conditions will also mean a 40 percent reduction by midcentury in California’s snowpack in the Sierra Nevada, which feeds the state’s reservoirs. What once fell as snow will instead fall as rain and immediately become runoff. This will lead to more severe droughts, according to the report.

Many Californians have already lived through the beginnings of these trends. The state this year logged its warmest August on record. And several of the most destructive fires in state history have happened in the last decade, including the wildfires last year in Los Angeles that were among the costliest disasters in U.S. history.

Abby Edwards, senior deputy director for the Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, which produced the assessment, said she hoped the report would alert communities and decision makers about where to focus their efforts as the climate continues to change.

The report, which weaves together existing and new, state-commissioned research, contains multiple scenarios based on different greenhouse gas emissions levels in the coming years, as well as recommendations for how to adapt to changing climate patterns.

“The future is not predetermined,” Ms. Edwards said in an interview.

The report comes as the Trump administration has been undermining California’s position as a national leader in environmental protection. As the world’s fourth-largest economy, California’s environmental regulations have influenced car and consumer goods manufacturers, and many of the state’s green policies have been adopted by other states in what’s known as the “California effect.”

Among the recent moves from the Trump administration: It ordered an oil company to restart a pipeline off Santa Barbara that caused one of the state’s largest oil spills in 2015; it announced $75 million for a new coal export terminal in Oakland that city officials have tried to stop for nearly a decade; and it has signaled that it could curb the power of the California Coastal Commission, which has been entrusted with protecting the state’s 840-mile shoreline for more than a half-century.

“As the Trump administration turns its back on science, California is doubling down on climate action, on protecting our communities, and on building a safer future,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.

The state’s assessments began in 2006 under former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger as a way to evaluate the specific threats of global warming on the state. This year’s assessment was the most extensive yet.

Beyond the statistics, the report also laid out how a changing climate could threaten beloved ways of life in California, such as skiing in the Sierra Nevada and going to the beach.

A longer summer means a shorter winter for California, and warmer temperatures are expected to blanket lower-elevation ski resorts with rain instead of snow. The snowpack is expected to fall by 60 percent by 2100.

The report also found that without major intervention, as much as three-quarters of California’s beaches could disappear — either seasonally or permanently — by 2100 because of coastal erosion. In that same time frame, sea level rise is expected to threaten $78 billion worth of property because of coastal flooding.

The state’s agricultural industry is expected to take a major hit as well.

Many crops require a certain number of hours of cold temperature to develop properly, and warmer temperatures could decrease fruit yields in some parts of the state by as much as 40 percent, according to the report.

At the same time, water shortages could mean that the number of acres that farmers irrigate could decline dramatically, including by up to 40 percent in the San Joaquin Valley, a major agricultural hub.

item.title: Trump Says Work on Disputed Golf Course Will Begin Immediately
item.description:
President Trump wrote on social media on Monday that work was “scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY” to overhaul a Washington golf course, escalating tensions with a federal judge who has prohibited the administration from cutting trees at the site.

Mr. Trump’s post came ahead of a morning showdown in federal court over the fate of the course.

Upon learning last week that the Interior Department had cleared hundreds of trees from the course, apparently in preparation for larger changes, the judge, Ana C. Reyes, had prohibited parks officials from taking down more trees until Oct. 26. She also requested that top administration officials appear at the hearing to discuss the issue.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump announced that the course, East Potomac Golf Links, would close for a 14-month renovation on Nov. 15, before returning to social media Monday morning to castigate the judge and announce the project would move forward.

He described Judge Reyes, an appointee of President Joseph R. Biden Jr., as “a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane.” The Justice Department had requested that audio be released of a hearing she conducted last week, in which she angrily took the Trump administration to task for removing trees with minimal notice.

Ahead of the hearing on Monday, Judge Reyes also issued a forceful opinion rebuffing calls by the Justice Department that she recuse herself from the case, denying that the record in the case demonstrated bias, as the administration had alleged.

She pointed out that she had consistently rejected what she described as premature requests by the group suing that she block work at the course. Instead, she wrote that she had approached the case as a “pragmatist” who had urged the parties in July to hammer out an agreement on their own, rather than pre-emptively halt work by court order. She had instead asked the government to provide notice before undertaking major work at the course.

“Between February 13, when this case was filed, and October 11, the court had not barred the government from taking any action in East Potomac, including tree removal,” she wrote.

“It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion,” she added. “But it is much harder to meet the demanding legal standard against a full record. By any objective measure, the Government fails to meet the standard for recusal.”

item.title: Supreme Court to Hear New Case on Race and School Admissions
item.description:
The Supreme Court announced on Monday that it would revisit the issue of race and school admissions, three years after it sharply restricted affirmative action in higher education.

The case involves four selective public middle schools in Montgomery County, Md., just outside the nation’s capital. A group of mostly Asian American parents sued the school system after it changed its admissions criteria, saying that the new rules unconstitutionally discriminated against Asian American students.

In 2023, the Supreme Court struck down race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina. The justices did not address other school policies intended to diversify student bodies that do not explicitly address race.

Since then the court has declined to hear several other challenges to admissions criteria at elite public schools, including one from Virginia and another from the military academy at West Point.

It takes the votes of four justices to grant review, however, and several justices had previously signaled their interest in continuing to explore the implications of the court’s decision affecting higher education. In the Virginia case, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. dissented, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, saying the court should have taken the case.

The justices also agreed on Monday to hear a challenge to federal bans on home distillation of whiskey and other spirits. An Ohio engineer had brought a lawsuit against a nearly 160-year-old federal ban on home distilling, in a case that will test 1860s-era prohibitions. The two cases will be added to the justices’ calendar for oral argument next year and decided before the Supreme Court’s term ends in late June or early July.

In the admissions case, the Maryland school district adopted a new lottery system for selecting eligible fifth graders for four highly competitive magnet middle schools after the coronavirus pandemic.

To be placed in a pool of eligible students, a candidate must have received an A grade in certain subjects, performed above a fourth-grade level in reading or math and scored in the 85th percentile on a standardized test adjusted for “local norms” such as the socioeconomic status of a specific elementary school population.

Students from schools with high poverty rates, for instance, are compared to other students from high-poverty schools.

In court filings, school officials described the process as “a race-neutral, race-blind lottery” adopted after abandoning an in-person exam because of pandemic constraints.

A group of families known as the Association for Education Fairness sued, arguing the lottery unconstitutionally discriminated against Asian American students. The families told the court that Asian American students who attended a high-performing elementary school “disproportionately must obtain substantially higher” standardized test scores to be eligible for the lottery than students of other races who attend lower-performing schools.

In response, school officials noted that at two of the county’s four magnet middle schools, the proportion of Asian Americans among admitted students increased in the first year of the new admissions policy.

A district court judge in Maryland dismissed the challenge, finding no evidence that the policy was enacted with a discriminatory intent. The judge said the policy was meant to account for economic disparities across different schools — a consideration the judge said was “wholly permissible.”

“Alleged disparity in treatment based on socioeconomic status alone does not make plausible discrimination on account of race,” wrote the judge, Paula Xinis.
